notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 32, drawn from the sources retrieved. Where a tradition or viewpoint could not be found in the search results, I note that omission.

---

## Title: “Of David. A Maskil.”

- **Maskil** – The term occurs in the title of thirteen psalms. The older commentators (Spurgeon, Gill) treat it as meaning “instructive” or “didactic” — a psalm intended to give understanding. Gill notes the Targum renders it “a good understanding” and the word properly means “instruction, or causing to understand.” Spurgeon says it was prefixed “that doubting saints might not imagine the Psalm to be the peculiar utterance of a singular individual, but might appropriate it to themselves as a lesson from the Spirit of God.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- The historic setting is generally understood as David’s experience after his sin with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah (2 Samuel 11–12), with Psalm 32 following Psalm 51 in the order of spiritual experience. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)

---

## v. 1: “Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered.”

- **The Beatitude**: Spurgeon calls this “the second Psalm of benediction” — Psalm 1 pictures the result of holy blessedness (the tree in full growth), Psalm 32 details the cause (forgiveness). He writes: “Blessedness is not in this case ascribed to the man who has been a diligent law keeper … but rather to a lawbreaker, who by grace most rich and free has been forgiven.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **“Forgiven” = “lifted off”**: Both Gill and the Pulpit Commentary note the Hebrew word means “taken off” or “borne away” — as a burden is lifted. Gill explains: “Sin was first taken off, and transferred from the sinner to Christ, the surety … and was bore by him, both guilt and punishment.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm) The Pulpit Commentary says the “transgression” is “lifted up, taken away.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **“Covered”**: Spurgeon says it is covered by God “as the ark was covered by the mercy seat, as Noah was covered from the flood.” Gill explains it is not covered by the sinner’s own works (“a covering too narrow”) but by Christ — His blood, and the robe of Christ’s righteousness. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm; https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **Three words for sin, three for pardon**: David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/Charismatic) notes David uses three different Hebrew words for sin (*transgression*, *sin*, *iniquity*) and three different words for what God does (*forgiven*, *covered*, *does not impute*), showing the completeness of God’s forgiveness. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- **Reformed view (Ligonier)**: The covering image recalls “God’s first act of grace after the fall … to provide clothes to cover the shame of our first parents (Gen. 3:21).” Forgiveness is tied to imputation — our sins imputed to Christ, His righteousness imputed to us. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joy-forgiveness)

---

## v. 2: “Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him, in whose spirit there is no deceit.”

- **Non-imputation**: Gill explains the Hebrew can mean “does not think of it” — God does not reckon sin to the believer’s account, having imputed it to Christ. Paul cites this verse in Romans 4:6–8 as proof of “righteousness imputed without works.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm) Spurgeon adds: “Certain divines froth at the mouth with rage against imputed righteousness, be it ours to see our sin not imputed.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **Reformed emphasis (Ligonier)**: “We are justified by Christ in that, by faith alone, our sins are imputed to Him for judgment on Calvary. His righteousness is then imputed to our record (2 Cor. 5:21).” The forgiveness David celebrates “utterly destroys the righteousness of works” (Calvin). “They only are blessed who rely upon God’s mercy.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-forgiveness)
- **“No deceit”**: Spurgeon says the forgiven person has been “taught to deal honestly with himself, his sin, and his God.” Those justified from fault are sanctified from falsehood — “a liar is not a forgiven soul.” Gill sees this as pointing to “internal sanctification,” completing the description of the happy (blessed) man. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: “Iniquity” is the internal defilement of the soul. It cannot be removed at once, but God can “not impute” it — then “in God’s sight the man is clean; it is as though the iniquity were not there.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal)**: “The prior life of sin and double-living was over for David … The forgiven life needs no more deceit to cover one’s ways.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)

---

## v. 3: “When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long.”

- **The misery of unconfessed sin**: David now recounts his own experience. “When I kept silent” means the period when he refused to confess his sin — likely the months between his adultery/murder and Nathan’s confrontation (2 Samuel 12). The Pulpit Commentary specifies: “The time spoken of is that which immediately followed the commission of the adultery, and which continued until Nathan uttered the words, ‘Thou art the man!’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Physical effects**: Spurgeon vividly describes: “While we smother our sin it rages within, and like a gathering wound swells horribly and torments terribly.” David “roared” — his voice “resembled the hoarse roaring of a wounded beast.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php) Guzik notes the stress of a double life made him “feel old, oppressed, and dry.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- **Gill** adds that David’s “bones waxed old” through this groaning — not under a sense of sin at first but under severe affliction, “not considering that sin lay at the bottom.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)** frames it: “We can harden our hearts for a time, but eventually guilt becomes a heavy burden … When the Spirit of God brings the burden of sin into our lives, it is not to be dismissed … It is an act of God, a painful act of God.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/honest-confession)

---

## v. 4: “For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat. Selah.”

- **God’s heavy hand**: David recognizes his suffering as directly from God. JFB: “thy hand — of God, or power in distressing him (Ps 38:2).” The Pulpit Commentary: “David sees now that his sufferings at this time came from God, and were a part of the punishment of his sin. They continued without intermission both by day and by night.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/32.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **“Moisture” / vitality drained**: JFB explains “moisture” as “vital juices of the body, the parching heat of which expresses the anguish of the soul.” The Pulpit Commentary: “the vital principle, which had been strong in him, was changed — burnt up and exhausted — by the heat of God’s wrath.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/32.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Ligonier’s wadi imagery**: Palestine has wadis (seasonal rivers) that dry up in summer and then experience flash floods when rains return. “Without pardon, our souls are dried up and subject to the waters of divine judgment.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joy-forgiveness)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal)** adds an important pastoral note: “David’s dryness and misery were actually a good thing. They demonstrated that he was in fact a son of God, and that the covenant God would not allow him to remain comfortable in habitual or unconfessed sin. One who feels no misery or dryness in such a state has far greater concerns for time and eternity.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- **Selah**: A pause for reflection. Spurgeon remarks, “It was time to change the tune, for the notes are very low in the scale.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)

---

## v. 5: “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and You forgave the guilt of my sin. Selah.”

- **Confession brings immediate forgiveness**: The turning point of the psalm. JFB: “A prompt fulfilment of the purposed confession is followed by a prompt forgiveness.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/32.htm)
- **Three words for sin again**: David uses “sin,” “iniquity,” and “transgressions” — matching the three terms from vv. 1–2 — showing his confession covered the full scope of his guilt. Gill: “his confession being of the same extent with pardon.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **Confession not the cause of pardon**: Gill is careful: “When confession of sin, and remission of it, are thus put together, the sense is not that confession of sin is the cause of pardon … it is not for the sake of a sinner’s confession of sin, but for Christ’s sake, that sin is forgiven; but this is the way in which it is enjoyed.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **Guzik (Pentecostal)**: “David’s confession of sin did not earn forgiveness of his sins, but he did receive it … David confessed and experienced this forgiveness immediately, just as the prodigal son confessed and was immediately forgiven. There was no probation, no wait-and-see period.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The confession may have been inward (“an inward confession, such as is accompanied with painful repentance and sorrow”) or outward. Forgiveness followed “without any interval.” However, the Pulpit Commentary adds that this forgiveness “did not preclude the exaction of a penalty required for the justification of God’s ways to man (2 Samuel 12:14)” — meaning David still bore temporal consequences. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Spurgeon**: “When the soul determines to lay low and plead guilty, absolution is near at hand … God’s pardons are deep and thorough: the knife of mercy cuts at the roots of the ill weed of sin.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)

---

## v. 6: “Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found. Surely when great waters rise, they will not come near.”

- **Encouragement for others**: David’s experience becomes a pattern. JFB: “For this — that is, my happy experience.” The godly are encouraged to seek the Lord likewise. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/32.htm)
- **“While You may be found”**: Spurgeon warns: “There is, however, a set time for prayer, beyond which it will be unavailing; between the time of sin and the day of punishment mercy rules the hour, and God may be found, but when once the sentence has gone forth pleading will be useless.” Gill interprets it not as a limited day of grace for individuals but as “a time of need, of soul distress.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **“Great waters”**: A metaphor for overwhelming trouble or divine judgment. JFB says it “denotes great danger (Ps 18:17; 66:12).” The Pulpit Commentary: the waters “shall not approach such a man to injure him.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/32.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Ligonier**: The “rush of great waters” is connected to the wadi flash-flood image from v. 4 — the flood of God’s wrath that the forgiven person is rescued from. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/joy-forgiveness)

---

## v. 7: “You are my hiding place. You protect me from trouble; You surround me with songs of deliverance. Selah.”

- **God as hiding place**: Spurgeon notes the dramatic reversal: “Observe that the same man who in the fourth verse was oppressed by the presence of God, here finds a shelter in him. See what honest confession and full forgiveness will do! The gospel of substitution makes him to be our refuge who otherwise would have been our judge.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php) Precept Austin picks up the same theme: David “exchanged hiding his sins for a HIDING PLACE in the Sin Coverer.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/god_our_hiding_place)
- **“Songs of deliverance”**: Spurgeon calls this “a golden sentence! The man is encircled in song, surrounded by dancing mercies … Before him hope sounds the cymbals, and behind him gratitude beats the timbrel.” Gill connects these songs to the voices of angels (citing Aben Ezra). (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **Utley (Baptist)** notes a play on God’s hand: “in judgment it was heavy (Ps 32:4; Ps 38:2) but in confession it protected him (Ps 32:6-7).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/psalms-32.html)

---

## v. 8: “I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you.”

- **Who is speaking?** A notable interpretive divide:
  - **God as speaker** (Spurgeon, JFB, Guzik, most evangelicals): “Here the Lord is the speaker, and gives the psalmist an answer to his prayer. Our Saviour is our instructor.” (Spurgeon) Guzik: “David prophetically spoke in God’s voice unto His people.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
  - **David as speaker** (Pulpit Commentary, some older critics): The Pulpit Commentary argues that “such a sudden intrusion of a Divine utterance, without any notice of a change of speaker, is without parallel in the Psalms.” Instead, David himself speaks, fulfilling his promise in Psalm 51:13 to “teach transgressors Your ways.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **“Guide you with My eye”**: Spurgeon explains it as the attentiveness of a servant to a master’s glance: “As servants take their cue from the master’s eye, and a nod or a wink is all that they require, so should we obey the slightest hints of our Master, not needing thunderbolts to startle our incorrigible sluggishness.” Guzik uses the same illustration: a butler who needs only a glance from his master to know he wants the salt. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- Gill notes that if David is the speaker, the meaning is that he will instruct others in the way of attaining the blessedness he has described — “by directing them to take the steps he did; namely, to go to the Lord, and acknowledge and confess their sins.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)

---

## v. 9: “Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding; they must be controlled with bit and bridle to make them come to you.”

- **Stubbornness versus willing obedience**: The horse and mule are used as examples of animals that lack understanding and must be forced. Spurgeon: “We ought to be as a feather in the wind, wafted readily in the breath of the Holy Spirit, but alas! we lie like motionless logs … Those cutting bits of affliction show how hard mouthed we are.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Israel is being warned not to be stiff-necked like a restive horse or mule. The animals “are excusable, since they ‘have no understanding’ — Israel would be inexcusable, since it had the gift of reason.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Guzik**: The horse and mule “need the bit and bridle, and sometimes rigorous training, before they are useful to the master.” God prefers willing, attentive obedience over forced compliance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- **On the obscure final clause** (“lest they come near unto you” / “else they will not come near you”): The Pulpit Commentary notes the Hebrew is obscure — possibly meaning “Lest they come too near to thee” and do damage (like a horse tossing its head and striking the rider), or “Else they will not come near to thee” (until bridled). JFB renders it “because they will not come … unless forced by bit and bridle.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/psalms/32.htm)

---

## v. 10: “Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD.”

- **Two ways contrasted**: This verse sets the wicked and the trusting believer in stark contrast. Spurgeon: “He who sows sin will reap sorrow in heavy sheaves … Faith in God is the great charmer of life’s cares, and he who possesses it, dwells in an atmosphere of grace, surrounded with the bodyguard of mercies.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **“Loving devotion” / “mercy” (hesed)**: God’s covenant faithfulness surrounds — even encompasses — the one who trusts. Gill: “he that trusteth in the Lord … mercy shall compass him about … as the Israelites were surrounded with the pillar of cloud, and enclosed in the arms of everlasting love.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/32.htm)
- **Guzik**: David “understood what it was to live (at least for a season) as the wicked, and the sorrows that came with it.” His renewed experience of mercy is the basis of his testimony. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)

---

## v. 11: “Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones; shout for joy, all you upright in heart.”

- **Joy as duty**: Spurgeon: “Happiness is not only our privilege, but our duty. Truly we serve a generous God, since he makes it a part of our obedience to be joyful.” He adds a warning against cold propriety: “It is to be feared that the church of the present day, through a craving for excessive propriety, is growing too artificial.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **“Righteous” and “upright in heart”**: These describe the forgiven. Spurgeon: “Note how the pardoned are represented as upright, righteous, and without guile; a man may have many faults and yet be saved, but a false heart is everywhere the damning mark.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: “David’s psalms almost always end with a note of joy … The present psalm, though reckoned among the penitential ones, both begins and ends with joyful utterances.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Guzik** lists five reasons for the rejoicing: “the blessedness of forgiveness, redemption from guilt, release from hypocrisy, God’s protection, and His guidance.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The search results did not yield substantial, distinctively different interpretations *by tradition* on Psalm 32. Most traditions read it similarly:

- **Reformed** (Ligonier, Sproul): Strong emphasis on imputation — the non-imputation of sin as the flip side of the imputation of Christ’s righteousness. This psalm is read through Romans 4 and seen as a premier proof-text for justification by faith alone apart from works. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/blessing-forgiveness)
- **Baptist** (Spurgeon, Gill, Utley): Also strongly imputation-centred. Spurgeon explicitly ties non-imputation to the imputed righteousness of Christ and defends it against those who “froth at the mouth with rage against imputed righteousness.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps032.php)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik): Emphasises the experiential and emotional dimensions — the misery of unconfessed sin, the immediate relief of confession, and the restoration of intimate fellowship where God guides “with His eye.” No clear doctrinal divergence from the Reformed/Baptist reading on the core points. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-32/)
- **Anglican** (Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott): Tends toward the historical-critical question (e.g., the speaker in v. 8, the dating relative to 2 Samuel). Also notes that forgiveness did not mean the removal of temporal penalties (2 Sam. 12:14). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/32.htm)
- **Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, and Catholic/Orthodox distinctives** on Psalm 32 could not be retrieved within the search and fetch limits of this research.
